opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's basically right, and it's actually one of the most useful analogies we have for thinking about AI.

If you're a biotech company and you've developed a new drug, you can't just start selling it at the corner pharmacy because you personally feel confident it's safe. You have to go to the FDA and make the case, with clinical trials and data, that the benefits outweigh the risks. The burden of proof is on the company, not on the public or the government to prove it's dangerous. And crucially, nobody thinks this is radical. Nobody says the FDA is crushing innovation in biotech. The biotech industry is thriving, partly *because* people trust that the products are safe.

Of course the system isn't perfect. People have legitimate criticisms that it can be too slow in some cases, or too bureaucratic. But the core principle, that you need to demonstrate safety before you release something powerful enough to hurt a lot of people, is something almost everyone agrees on. We do the same with airplanes, nuclear reactors, even sandwiches; a sandwich shop has more safety regulation than many of the companies building frontier AI.

That's what strikes me as so strange about the current situation with AI. We're talking about technology that the people building it say could pose risks on par with pandemics or nuclear war, and yet there's no equivalent of an FDA requiring them to demonstrate that it's safe and controllable before deployment. The burden of proof is backwards. Right now it's on the rest of us to prove that something is dangerous after it's already out there.

So I'd say the FDA model isn't a perfect template to copy line by line, but the principle behind it, safety standards first, then release, is exactly what we should be applying to the most powerful AI systems. It's not anti-technology. It's the same approach that made medicine trustworthy, and it would make AI trustworthy too.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's one of the most important analogies we have, honestly, for thinking about how to handle AI. Because the claim itself is just true as a matter of fact: if you want to sell a new drug in the United States, you can't just put it on the market and see what happens. You have to go to the FDA, you have to demonstrate through clinical trials that the benefits outweigh the risks, and the burden of proof is on you, the company, not on the public. And we have the same thing for airplanes with the FAA, for nuclear reactors, for cars, for food. Basically every other powerful technology that can hurt people, we've decided as a society that the people making money from it have to show it's safe before they get to deploy it.

And what's striking to me is that AI is the glaring exception. Right now, if OpenAI or Google or Anthropic or whoever wants to release a system that they themselves say might be able to help someone build a bioweapon, there is no equivalent of the FDA they have to go to. There's no requirement to demonstrate safety first. It's the Wild West. If a biotech company said, "We've made this new molecule, we're not totally sure what it does, we're just going to release it to a hundred million people and see," everybody would recognize that as insane. But in AI we've somehow normalized exactly that.

Now, people push back and say the FDA is slow, it's bureaucratic, it kills innovation. And sure, there are legitimate criticisms of how it's implemented. But notice that nobody seriously argues we should abolish it and go back to the era of snake oil and thalidomide. The pharmaceutical industry is enormous and profitable and innovative despite having safety standards, and I'd argue partly because of them, because people actually trust the products. So I don't buy the argument that safety standards and innovation are opposed. I think the drug analogy actually shows the opposite.

The deeper point is this: FDA approval is basically a mechanism for making sure humanity stays in control of a powerful technology. We decide what gets released, not the technology, not just whoever happens to be first. And that's exactly the kind of mechanism I think we desperately need for AI, especially as we're moving toward systems that are more capable than us in more and more domains. If you're building something that could do more damage than a dangerous drug, the bar for proving it's safe should be higher, not nonexistent.

astra-6.text:
I think the basic principle is a very sensible one: if you want to release something that could seriously harm people, you should demonstrate that it’s sufficiently safe before you release it. We don’t generally say, “Let’s put this drug on the market, and if a lot of people die, we’ll figure out what went wrong.” We put the burden of proof on the company developing it.

Now, saying that every potentially dangerous biological or medical product requires FDA approval is too broad. The requirements depend on what the product is. But the underlying idea is what matters here: when the risks are substantial, testing before release is appropriate. And I think it’s entirely reasonable to ask why we shouldn’t apply that same principle to increasingly powerful AI.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the basic principle makes sense: if you’re going to release something that could seriously harm people, the burden should be on you to demonstrate that it’s sufficiently safe before you release it. FDA approval isn’t a guarantee that nothing will ever go wrong, but it means we don’t simply let companies experiment on the public and deal with the consequences afterward.

The analogy to AI is that we should ask why the burden of proof would be reversed. If a company is developing a system that could pose serious risks to society, why should the public have to prove it’s dangerous, rather than the company having to demonstrate that it’s safe?
